general.temas: The congressional elections and the 2028 presidential race feature in The New York Times, The Washington Post and Los Angeles Times. The conviction over the Palisades fire appears in The Washington Post and The Wall Street Journal. Climate, courts and crime and accidents are also recurring topics. The New York Post alone highlights the release of records on the health effects of the September 11 attacks.
general.motivo_crispacion: Tensions are moderate: the election results are fueling debate among Republicans about their defeats and Trump’s role, while Democrats look ahead to 2028. There is also tension between the administration and environmental groups over the planned detonation in Iowa, as well as legal disputes related to government projects. Internationally, climate talks have collapsed over disagreement on fossil fuels. Stories about culture, recipes, sports and medical advances offer a calmer counterpoint.

The New York Times.resumen:
- Democrats win 258 seats in the House of Representatives and several notable victories.
- Republicans debate the causes of their defeat and Trump’s role.
- COP31 talks collapse over disagreements on fossil fuels.
- The front page covers the war in Ukraine, Stephen Miller’s claims and the dispute over AI chips.
- It also includes stories on AI safety, Thanksgiving recipes and movies.
The New York Times.motivo_populismo: The tone is largely informational, although expressions such as “crushing defeat,” “stunning reversal” and “apocalypse” add drama and sensationalism.
The New York Times.sesgo: The selection highlights Democratic victories and divisions and false claims attributed to Republican figures. At the same time, it includes a story about Melania Trump’s diplomatic role and subjects unrelated to electoral politics.

The Washington Post.resumen:
- The Army plans a detonation in Iowa despite an environmental lawsuit; another story examines how Trump is pushing ahead with projects despite court setbacks.
- Congresswoman-elect Angela Gonzales-Torres explains her opposition to Jeffries; the possible presidential ambitions of Vance and Rubio are also examined.
- A man was convicted of starting the Palisades fire, which destroyed more than 6,800 buildings.
- The front page looks back at Jackie Kennedy’s bloodstained suit and an interracial kiss on American television.
- Other stories cover a National Guard member’s recovery, medical services using drones, obituaries and personal accounts.
The Washington Post.motivo_populismo: The tone is largely informational, although expressions such as “keeps losing in court” and the reference to the “blood-spattered” suit add drama; there is no apparent appeal to the people against the elites.
The Washington Post.sesgo: The selection includes critical scrutiny of the Trump administration’s conduct in the courts. It also gives space to human-interest, cultural and scientific stories; these headlines do not establish an overall partisan orientation.

The Wall Street Journal.resumen:
- New York’s billionaire police chief and its socialist mayor maintain a partnership described as unlikely.
- A jury finds a man guilty of starting the Palisades fire; in South Carolina, several officers face misconduct charges in a fatal shooting.
- The front page covers cellphone bans in schools, shorter college degree programs, lawsuits by parents and a proposed rule on racial discrimination.
- Ken Griffin gives $3 billion to Carnegie Mellon; there are also leadership and team changes at major law firms.
- A feature portrays life aboard an aircraft carrier, while another story reports the death of Fiona, the Cincinnati hippo.
The Wall Street Journal.motivo_populismo: The tone is largely informational, although contrasts such as “billionaire” and “socialist” and expressions such as “worst fear” add drama.
The Wall Street Journal.sesgo: The selection pays attention to institutions, vast fortunes, education and legal affairs. There is no clear partisan orientation in the headlines provided.

Los Angeles Times.resumen:
- Threat of extreme flooding on the California coast and advice to avoid travel.
- Democrats look to 2028 after the congressional elections, with Texas a competitive state.
- Saudi Arabia seeks alternatives to U.S. weapons amid attacks by Iran and the Houthis.
- Experts propose buying coastal homes and renting them out before retreating as sea levels rise.
- Local incidents: a detention by immigration agents, an earthquake, an explosion at a landfill and a body found in the Los Angeles River.
Los Angeles Times.motivo_populismo: The tone is largely informational, although expressions such as “threat of extreme flooding,” “monumental change” and “smashing a window” add drama; there is no apparent appeal to the people against the elites.
Los Angeles Times.sesgo: The selection has a strong local focus on California, with attention to environmental risks and local incidents. Political coverage centers on Democrats’ electoral prospects, though this alone does not establish a partisan orientation for the front page.

New York Post.resumen:
- New York releases 84,000 additional documents on air quality and toxic effects after 9/11.
- An off-duty police officer shoots his partner, also an officer, and then himself.
- Soccer player Leandro Paredes collapses during an interview; stories about the Yankees and the Kansas City Current’s celebration also feature prominently.
- The front page covers commercial growth in an area of Midtown and the planned opening of a new Los Tacos location.
- Other pieces cover decor and trauma, Thanksgiving dishes, a celebrity pregnancy and a promotion for trading on Kalshi.
New York Post.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “horrific” and “massive trove of secret records” add drama, although there is no apparent confrontation between the people and the elites.
New York Post.sesgo: The selection combines a strong focus on New York with crime and incidents, sports, celebrities and promotional content. Some headlines emphasize drama or curiosity; there is no clear political bias.

opiniones.comunista:
The collapse of COP31 reveals, in my view, a central contradiction of our time: while California’s coast faces extreme flooding, fossil fuel interests continue to obstruct a transition away from them. The transition cannot be left to the market or paid for with working-class jobs and housing. I advocate collectively owned energy, public investment and decent jobs to transform production.

The Democrats’ large House majority opens up an opportunity, but changing the composition of Congress does not in itself change who owns the wealth and sets economic priorities. I would judge it by its willingness to strengthen public services, protect working people and confront the power of big capital. Without working-class organization, election promises risk remaining just promises.
opiniones.anarquista:
The Democratic House majority can change specific decisions, but let’s not confuse a change of parties in power with emancipation. I don’t want to limit my freedom to choosing who governs: I want those of us who share a neighborhood or a workplace to be able to decide directly about our lives, without bosses or untouchable representatives.

The failure of COP31 shows the limits of entrusting the climate’s future to negotiations among states, some of which defend fossil fuels. In the face of floods threatening the California coast, the response cannot be reduced to waiting for another summit: we need neighborhood networks of mutual aid, preparedness and decisions made by the affected communities. Self-management does not by itself eliminate the danger, but it allows us to face its consequences without surrendering our ability to act to those who concentrate power.
opiniones.liberal:
The Democratic victory in the House deserves respect: the voters have spoken. But a majority does not automatically make every expansion of government good policy. I would ask the new lawmakers for low taxes and a limited state that leaves families and businesses to decide how to use more of what they earn. Personal responsibility requires precisely the space to choose, start a business and face the consequences.

I also welcome the fact that some universities are offering three-year degree programs to reduce costs. It is an example of how competition and innovation can expand opportunities without always waiting for a solution from Washington. And in the face of COP31’s failure, I believe protecting the climate requires clear rules and accountability for harm, but also freedom for markets to develop better technologies. Replacing innovation with blanket bans can make energy more expensive without solving the problem.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
I see the Democratic victory as a warning that the right cannot dismiss by blaming a single leader. If we want to regain citizens’ trust, we must defend national sovereignty with concrete proposals and be accountable when we govern. Borders must be controlled rigorously, but also through clear procedures subject to the law: security does not require unlimited powers.

I am also concerned about the Chinese espionage campaign to obtain advanced chips. We cannot leave strategic technologies at the mercy of commercial interests or blindly trust economic elites to put the country before business. And I welcome the consideration of limits on phones in schools: education requires attention, discipline and authority. A strong nation protects its borders, its industrial capacity and the institutions that pass on its values.
opiniones.centro:
The Democratic House majority is an opportunity, not a blank check. I would celebrate the victory by starting now to work with those willing to reach agreements, even across the aisle. Governing well requires lasting reforms, not just preparing for the next election.

I am concerned that the administration intends to press ahead with a detonation in Iowa while an environmental lawsuit is pending. An emergency must not become an excuse to evade judicial scrutiny. And the failure of COP31 is a reminder that we need a negotiated energy transition, with credible targets and support for affected communities. The market can drive innovation, but it is no substitute for public regulation or social protection. That combination, gradual and demanding, strikes me as more useful than promising instant solutions.
